text: — Well then, wait while I tell you how Uncle Ganyo and I went to the exhibition in Prague — said Tsvyatko with a smile.
— Bravo, Tsvyatko! — we all shouted. — We’ve been waiting for this for so long!
Tsvyatko began:

— If you remember, we set out from Sofia with an entire train of our own carriages and our own locomotive. Carriages only of first and second class, brand-new, just arrived from Europe, impeccably clean and comfortable. In the same carriage there were compartments of both first and second class. A whole crowd — were we 160 people, I don’t remember. Old and young, women, men, children, and even infants. (Oh, those infants!...)

Who like us! What pride it was that we were setting off for the exhibition with our own train. Let them see, we said to ourselves, the Europeans, that Bulgaria does not sleep. But above all we were puffed up with the novelty, with the modern construction, and with the cleanliness of the carriages. But for how long, do you think, did we enjoy the patriotic charm of the superiority of our carriages and the thought that we would astonish Europe with our progress? While they were seeing us off at the station, while we were passing the Slivnitsa and Dragoman positions — the fields of our glorious victories — our enthusiasm grew in proportion to the emptying of the bottles and baskets of provisions, with which the practical tourists had supplied themselves in abundance. “Of course, we’ll take some snacks with us; why should we give our money to the Serbs?” — cried the patriotically inspired and Pleven-wine-fueled Bay Ganyo. But when we drew near to Tsaribrod and it began to grow dark, when they tried to light the carriages and it turned out they had forgotten to prepare the lamps, when it grew completely dark, when the children began to get frightened and to cry — oh, then little by little, as if with the slipping away of Bulgarian territory, our patriotic enthusiasm was slipping away too. Some smiled sadly, others smiled covertly and sarcastically (we were not only Bulgarians), others protested; even Bay Ganyo whispered in my ear: “Does a pig understand spring water!” Some others let loose unmistakable curses at a foreigner serving in the administration of our railways. Supported by the last ones, Bay Ganyo shouted: “Don’t I know that we’re not to blame, it’s those foreigners again, may the devil take them! They did it on purpose to disgrace us! And do you know, it’s all out of envy! They’re all like that!”

At those words he looked so sharply at one of the foreigners that he made him cough and move into the other compartment. When we stopped at the station in Tsaribrod, it was completely dark in the carriages; we could not see one another. We got agitated, got a little angry, then turned it into laughter. A whole lot of jokes and barbs were aimed at our railway officials. Cries were heard: “Give us candles, people, you’ve frightened the children!”, “Hey, uncle, go buy us a pound of candles, we’ll give you a tip,” “Come on, at least give us one tallow candle.” Only Bay Ganyo would not admit that Bulgarians could be to blame for this disorder.

— That one there, do you see him — he was saying, after they brought several plain candles, and pointed at one of our compatriot foreigners, — you’d pour tar over him, just to set him on fire. Can that be endured, eh! Never mind the darkness, who cares about that — but we’ve made a disgrace of ourselves before the Serbs. There he is, do you see him, a Serbian official — the man is laughing. Laughing, indeed! But the stirred-up patriotism did not allow Bay Ganyo to endure a Serb’s smirking at him, so he frowned back at him:
— Well, why are you laughing over there, hey! And he wanted to jump off the wagon and go sort things out with the Serb. Heroic blood!
— Shh... Stand still, Bay Ganyo — the passengers urged him, — don’t make a scandal. Bear in mind that you are entering Serbia...
— Well, so what, if I’m entering Serbia! Will they scare me? What about Slivnitsa? What about “back, brothers” — and from Bay Ganyo’s mouth there flew out an oath like a bomb.
— What has the Serb done to you, that our wagons were dark! — the others reassured him.
— Who? Him? I know them! — replies Bay Ganyo and shakes his head.

They handed out one candle per compartment. Some of the lamps, I think, they managed to adjust and light. The train set off. The passengers dripped hot tallow onto the windows and fixed the candles in place. This was the first   B u l g a r i z a t i o n   of the new carriages. The second Bulgarization took place on the very first night: all the toilets (excuse me, gentlemen) turned into cesspools.

Anyway, we passed through Serbia. But don’t think that we passed through it all quietly and modestly. Oh no! The Bulgarian is no fool! Wherever he had the opportunity, Bay Ganyo did not miss a chance to sting the Serbs, to remind them of Slivnitsa. In Niš and Belgrade even, he asked all the clerks and porters: “Aren’t you Bulgarian, tell the truth? You are all Bulgarians, but you are Serbianizing yourselves.”

We set off through Hungary!... Here, too, the wheels of one carriage caught fire! May the ashma take you and your craftsmen! We stopped for a long time. They poured water, put it out, lit it again, smoldered... at last we set off. And the Hungarians — laughter! They knew! — Bulgarian tourists!... And at another place this carriage caught fire again — at last they left it to the devil for repairs.

Bay Ganyo, an experienced man who had traveled before, was telling his less sophisticated companions:

— Now we’ll head for Pest. Once we pass Pest — Vienna; Prague is beyond Vienna. I’ve been all over those places — I know them like the back of my hand.

We did not stop at the small stations. At the large ones we stopped only long enough for them to open a line for us. Rich Moravia drew everyone’s attention. The beautifully cultivated valleys, the splendid gardens, the countless factories and plants made even Bay Ganyo admit Moravia’s superiority over our fatherland: “We work too, but these fellows are no slouches either, ah, no slouches, the fellows know their stuff.” But then, remembering that he had gotten carried away in praise, he added: “But it’s all for nothing. They do the work, and the German eats it.”

There was no getting through the journey without comedies. We — I, Vancho, Filyo, and Ivantsov’s son (I don’t believe you know him) — occupied a first-class compartment; in the adjoining second-class section settled Bay Ganyo with several companions, richly supplied with provisions. Bay Ganyo, in his haste, it seems, had forgotten to put any breakfast in his saddlebags. “Well, after all, we’re Bulgarians, we’ll look after one another. From this bit of bread, from that bit of cheese — one can get by. Well then!” And indeed, he got by very well. His companions treated him to food and drink — he treated them to the hottest patriotism, mixed with appetite and thirst. But everything has an end. At last our neighbors’ provisions ran out, the gallons were emptied. (To avoid a gross mistake, I must correct myself: the gallons were emptied already when we were flying over Slivnitsa and Dragoman with “Long live Bulgaria, hurrah! Let me wet my mouth, hey, hurrah!”)

Bai Ganyo began to edge closer to our compartment. At first he looked for various pretexts: now he would ask for a match, now for a glass of cognac — because his stomach was hurting him — and then little by little he settled in, got used to us, and, so to speak, hardly ever left our little room. He forgot his companions, and why should he need them? — They had nothing at all — everything eaten, everything drunk — whereas with us, thank God, there was always something to be found — we bought things at the stations. Out of curiosity, Bai Ganyo never missed a chance to try the foreign products:
— What is this, is it grapes? Bravo! Look! Give me a little bunch. Mmm! Nice! Bravo! Curiosity made him get acquainted in this way with our breakfasts, with our cognac, with our tobacco cases.
— Is this cigarette case made of Caucasian silver? — inquired Bay Ganyo curiously, seeing one of us preparing to light up.
— It isn’t; it’s Viennese-made! — replies the owner.
— Is that so? Come, let me see it. T... t... t! Look! And there’s tobacco too, Bulgarian, right? Bravo! Wait, let me roll a cigarette. I’ve got cigarette papers; if you need them — I’m here!

That he was here, we felt quite clearly: by the smell of his boots, by the distinctive aroma of his sweaty body, and by his aggressive movement toward occupying the entire sofa. At first he sat on the edge of the sofa, then he began to sit more comfortably, and later three of us had to sit on one sofa, while Ivantsov’s son had to squeeze himself onto the edge of the other, so that Bay Ganyo would have the opportunity to take a horizontal position. And he never missed a chance. We agreed to try to see how far Bay Ganyo’s need for comfort could go, and he began quite candidly to feed our curiosity:

— Move over a little toward the edge so I can put my other leg up too. There! Bravo! Ahhh! Damn it! Bliss! Listen to what the machine is doing: thump-thump, thump-thump! It’s flying!... I love stretching out like this. Beyond narrow. And the comrades too — simple folks, what is there to talk to them about?... What are you eating over there, a pear? Bravo! Let’s see, lying here like this, can I eat a pear? Thanks! Where do you get these things?
— We’ll buy them — one of us replies with barely restrained restraint.
“Is that so? Bravo!” he approves, his mouth full of the juicy pear. “I like pears.”

Bai Ganyo, lulled by the monotonous blows of the locomotive, began to doze. I was thinking to myself what, what to do to him. At last a brilliant idea dawned on me. I made a prearranged sign to my companions and said: — Let us have a coffee, gentlemen. Hand over the spirit and the little stove.
— Coffee? — cried Bay Ganyo and jumped up from the sofa as if stung. — Is there any question?
— What coffee are we going to make, there’s no water — said Ivantsov’s son, with a theatrically affected voice.
— Water? — cried Bay Ganyo in the same voice. — Ask me for nothing but water. Right away! — And he flew out of the compartment.

We were doubled over with laughter. Ivantsi’s son stretched out and took up the whole sofa. Uncle Ganyo came back and puffed more than he needed to. He had to show us what labor and hardship he had endured for our good. In his hand, a little jug.

— Well, I found it, did you see? I searched through all the wagons! At last I saw a jug, I grabbed it right away, and a woman shouted at me: “Hey, give the water here, it’s for my child.” What was I to lie, what was I to lie, it came to me: “Excuse me, madam, someone over there fainted.” “Is that so,” says she. “Yes.” “Well then, quickly take him some water and bring the little jug back.” Stupid woman!... Phew! I’m all sweaty. Now then, a little coffee!
— Aren’t you ashamed, sir! — said one of the companions reproachfully, no longer able to restrain his indignation.

Bay Ganyo looked at him with a strained face, trying as visibly as possible to portray his sincere astonishment; then quite unexpectedly he said: — It occurred to me that the thing was a setup, but I said, well, let it be. So give me at least one cigarette and a little cognac.

“We gave him a cigarette and some cognac, and he went off to his own compartment, to the simple folk.” “Those learned men are terrible boors,” came Bay Ganyo’s voice a little later from the neighboring compartment; “I don’t know how they put up with such people in service. But wait, your Bay Ganyo will come back to Bulgaria, and then we’ll see who’s who.”

We were approaching the Czech border. With us were also the commissioners sent by the government to learn how to arrange an exhibition, so that they could arrange the Plovdiv one as well. One of them pinned small Bulgarian tricolors on the chests of all the passengers. Along the way, a rumor also spread that we would be greeted ceremoniously both at the border and in Prague; therefore, we were prepared for the reception — but what we saw in reality surpassed all our expectations.

Here is the border station, the locomotive is already whistling. We see, on the left and on the right of the railway line, people streaming toward the station. It was raining, and the running men, women, and children were carrying open umbrellas. We stopped. The platform was crowded with people. Immediately a band burst out with “Shumi Maritsa.” A choir then sang “Kde domov muj” to the endless delight of all of us, and especially of Bay Ganyo, who praised among us the Czech people for having studied quite well the tune of the Bulgarian folk song “Where is my home,” only they pronounced the words a little indistinctly, so it was not very well understood.

Blood rushes to my head with shame when I remember the behavior we displayed at that first meeting. Imagine, gentlemen: the town had gathered, people had come from the villages to welcome the Bulgarian brothers, they had brought music, a choir had come, a great many girls had lined up with bouquets in their hands, waiting for the brothers to get off the train so they could greet them, welcome them with words, with songs, with music, with bouquets; and the “brothers” had stuck their heads out of the windows and were looking! Believe me, believe me, gentlemen! The train windows, you should know, are narrow; one had stuck out his head, another was squeezed over his neighbor’s shoulder, a third was showing only half of his twisted face with one eye from below, and they were looking! — You could melt away! Ah, if only there had been a snapshot photograph! — The greeters were bewildered. They too did not know what to do — where to put the bouquets! The music stopped, the choir stopped too, and silence fell, along with mutual staring.

At one point, Bay Ganyo got down from the carriage. All the Czechs fixed their eyes on him and made way for him to pass, and he passed... My God! How grandly Bay Ganyo walked through the midst of hundreds of eyes and hands stretching out bouquets to him. He took a whole handful and twisted up his left mustache, thrust his elbows outward, coughed heavily, and glanced with one eye at the young lady who had held out her bouquet almost under his nose; he looked at her and waved the fingers of his left hand upward, as if to say: “Are you welcoming me, girl, are you welcoming me? Good, keep welcoming—I like it” — and went on his way without deigning to honor her by accepting her bouquet. The girl withdrew her hand in embarrassment. After a little while, Bay Ganyo reappeared, fastening not quite gracefully a part of his attire. Again they made way for him, again he twirled his left mustache, again he coughed, blew his nose with his fingers, and climbed into the carriage. The locomotive whistled and we set off.

So that none of you may think that I am exaggerating, that I am deliberately embellishing my story in order to caricature Bay Ganyo, I will tell you that, on the contrary, I am omitting certain things, because even now my heart tightens when I recall them. For example, I deliberately kept silent at the beginning about what picture our train presented already on the second day of our journey. Did I not mention to you that our tourists had taken the infants along with them as well; leaving aside the cries and screams, I will tell you that the lavatories had turned into laundries, where the children’s soiled little shirts and drawers were being washed, and the corridors of the carriages had become drying rooms for this laundry: they stretched ropes and hung out the not-so-well-washed drawers; they replaced the flags with which we were supposed to decorate our train; instead of the tricolor — white, green, and red — there shone in the sun a multitude of two-color flags — white and yellow. These beauties adorned our train even when we stopped at stations in Bohemia and the people, with music, with songs, with bouquets, with welcoming speeches by the mayors and other representatives, greeted us. These yellow-and-white flags fluttered on the ropes even when our leader, Mr. Vasilaki, deafened the Czech listeners with his thunderous sentimental speeches, and when Mr. Petko tickled the national vanity of the brotherly Czech people at every station with his oratorical words, from which, for those standing farther away, only the words could be clearly heard: “Brothers! Ivan Hus... Oh! Ivan Hus, brothers!” and when Bay Ganyo, indignant that the speeches made no mention of our historical giants, poked a teacher in the ribs with the words: “Teacher, say something too, eh, let’s show them who we are, now is the time, say something about Filip Totya, or about Krum the Terrible, or sing a song...” And the two-color flags kept on fluttering!...

Our entire journey from the Czech border to Prague was one triumphant procession; whether by towns or villages, across fields—wherever our train passed, hats flew up into the air and an endless “nazdar!” split the air.

I noticed a female worker in the field who, when she saw the men waving and throwing their hats, waved and waved her hands, then took off the kerchief from her head, whirled it in the air, and shouted: “Nazdaar!” Another thing: we were passing by a town (I don’t remember what it was called, and how could you remember it, we were stunned then), with people in the streets, people at the windows, on the trees, on the fences, even on the eaves. So in that town, I remember, I noticed in one place a new house being built, almost finished, and the beams of the eaves were piled up, on top of the eaves there was a long pole stuck in, decorated with greenery, and on top of it a flag (as with us, when they build houses): several workers up there, when they saw that all along the street from all the floors people were waving kerchiefs and shouting “nazdaar!”, ran along the beams to the top of the eaves, seized the pole with the flag and set out to pull it out in order to salute us, but, it seems, it was firmly fixed — they could not pull it out, but they shook it at the base enough so that it could flutter with a small amplitude to the left and right. These two cases — with the workers in the field and with the masons on the eaves — deeply moved me. It did not resemble our own: “The whole intelligentsia was splitting the air with frenetic hurrahs,” “Today the whole nation rejoices...”

We arrived at the station in Prague. On the platform we did not notice many people; there were only official greeters: the assistant to the mayor, if I am not mistaken, and the members of the exhibition committee. This reception seemed dull to me; we had grown used to triumph! But there was more to it than met the eye; people who know how things are arranged understand that when 160 people get off the train, if there is a crowd on the platform, they will mix together, get in each other’s way: it will turn into a mess of guests, hosts, and luggage, so they had left the platform empty and only a commission had appeared to welcome us.  

Then the greetings and speeches began again: on one side, “Bratri...! Bulhari...! Veliky slovansky... Cyrila Metodej”; on the other side, “Bratri, my jsme prsli poucit se u velkeho ceskeho naroda!”... on a third side: “Brothers! The great Ivan Hus!... Yes, brothers, Ivan Hus is great!” And Bay Ganyo, for his part, dissatisfied that they were mentioning only Cyril and Methodius, kept nudging the teacher again: “Say something too, teacher, eh? Don’t we have a few of our own? Say Asparuh, or go on, blow the flute — now’s the time!...”

Here they told us that everyone would go to the city club “Meshtanska Beseda,” and from there we would be assigned to lodgings. They ordered that our luggage be brought there. We set off. From the platform we enter the station hall, and what do you think! People! Black with people! Literally not even an egg could be dropped there. In the middle, a strip just wide enough for us to pass. On this side and that, ladies lined up with bouquets. All dressed for a holiday. And then there burst out a “nazdar!”, and they began handing us bouquets and showering us with flowers, and when we went out into the street and looked — my God! — as far as the eye could see: they had left only one strip for us, and everything else was jammed with people, and again rows of ladies, and again “nazdaaar! nazdaaar! hurraaa!” — and again a whole city of bouquets. — A royal welcome!... We sat down amid the shouts and flowers in carriages and set off. Now, how gracefully we sat and how we got mixed up with the households and the infants — I leave it to you to imagine! We were like people struck by the unexpected grand reception! We take off our hats to the left and right; then we remembered to take them off completely (when it comes to remembering, we remembered a lot, eh? We understand these things, the etiquette!). A smile had frozen on my convulsively trembling lips, and it seemed as though I wanted at once to laugh, to cry, and to sink through the earth!

We arrived at “Meshchanska beseda” and took the tables in the garden. We waited for our luggage to arrive and for us to be assigned to lodgings. Several cabmen waited, poor fellows, for a whole hour around the gates to be paid, but many of our tourists did not find it necessary to pay. “No big deal,” бай Ганьо would say, “what does it cost them to pay for the cabs? After all—we’re Slavs! Let them show their Slavness here, eh? Why, of course! Everything for free! Even grandma knows money talks! Only one plain thing—nazdar”...

The luggage arrived, and they began assigning us to lodgings. The people took care to find rooms for us. I won’t tell you about the quarrels with the cabmen, with the waiters in the club, with the ushers over being late or over the luggage being mixed up by mistake, about the discomforts of the lodgings, about the bargaining and other such things. Let us move with you for a minute into our room (don’t be afraid, madam). We settled four of us in a large room. We had every convenience. Our room looked onto the courtyard... On the opposite side the same number of stories rose up. At one point the maid who looked after us, Anushka, as she was taking the flowerpots from the windows so that she could close them, suddenly turned to me and, embarrassed, asked me, pointing with her eyes toward the windows opposite:

— Please, sir, is that gentleman also Bulgarian? Just look at what he is doing! His coat is black! Hairy like some savage! Ha-ha-ha-ha!

I look in the indicated direction and what do I see? Bay Ganyo, with the windows open, without drawing the curtains or blinds, having taken off his outer clothes, and at the very moment when I looked, he was grinning at our maid and stroking his hairy chest; it seems that with this he wanted to captivate her.

In the local newspapers, on the same day, greetings appeared for the dear (they had every right to be) guests — bratri Bulhari. The program was also printed, according to which we would visit the exhibition and the sights of the city of Prague. Reports were printed about our visits: where we had gone, how we had been received, how they had greeted us, what we had replied to them. The name of our guide, Mr. Vasilaki, was resounding; he earned this attention with his countless speeches. And to tell the truth, say what you will, but if it had not been for Mr. Vasilaki to smooth things over for them, we would have completely failed.

At the entrance to the exhibition we were greeted by members of the committee. And again speeches about the Czech people, about the Bulgarian people. Here, you see, they did not make the mistake of greeting us as Serbs, as the mistake, they say, that happened at the entrance to the Plovdiv Exhibition: the people of Sliven and Yambol were in constant antagonism—out of envy, out of rivalry, who knows why. The people of Sliven appear at the entrance to the Plovdiv Exhibition, and one of their committee members gives a speech, thinking them to be people from Yambol, and praises and praises: “The brave people of Yambol, the glorious people of Yambol!” And the people of Sliven sweat, cough into their hands, blink... A picture!...

We entered the exhibition. One of the committee led us to make a quick general survey of the main departments. Well, whom did he lead? — Our tourists — complete Englishmen!... Once those people got into the botanical department — there was no getting out!
— Ivancho, Ivancho, come, come here, look at the tulip, how big it is! Do you remember, your aunt has such a tulip! — calls one from one side.
— Mariyke, Mariyke, come, come here, look at the mimosa, this is mimosa, do you see? Do you remember in the little atlas I bought you for Easter? — calls another from the other side.
— Look, basil! C... c... c... The Czechs have basil too, bravo! — a third one chimes in, and they start looking at the basil.
— Well, I don’t see any geranium here — says Bay Ganyo in a dissatisfied voice. — Their business is simple if they don’t have geranium! Eeh, at our place! In the Balkans! Ah, damn it!
And the committee member, meanwhile, stood as if on thorns! They were waiting for the dear guests to finish speaking!...

I could not restrain myself; I left the botanical section and went to gape at the other pavilions. In my absence, the distinguished guests were photographed, and the next day the whole group appeared in an illustrated newspaper.

They took us to Hradčany, where the palaces of the Czech kings are. They showed us various historical little corners: the room where the council had met and the beginning of the Thirty Years’ War had been decided; the window through which the Czech patriots had been thrown into the abyss. They took us to the old city hall, to the old and the new museum. In our honor they gave an opera at the National Theatre, and a soirée at the “Citizens’ Club.” We went to Mr. Náprstek, a highly respected citizen, once compromised before the Austrian government, who had fled to America, made a fortune there, returned to Prague, and now, surrounded by honors and respect, is engaged in philanthropy. He has his own museum and library. Our host received us with all the warmth and hospitality of a Slav. Here the most heartfelt speeches were made. In one of the rooms there was a thick book in which visitors wrote down their names. At one moment, when many people had gathered around the book and everyone was hurrying to snatch the pen and immortalize his name, Bay Ganyo pulled me by the sleeve and asked impatiently: — Well, what are they signing up there for?

I, knowing in advance that no pretext for signing up would satisfy Bay Ganyo unless something came of it before the godfather, said to him jokingly: whoever does not wish to continue wandering about the antiquities of Prague may sign his name in this book and have lunch at pana Naprstka’s.

— Is that so? — cried Bay Ganyo. — To hell with their antiquities, give me the pen here! Give it, come on, give me the pen quickly! Can’t I use a pencil? Give it, give it, I’m in a hurry! — and he began to force his way with his elbows toward the table on which the big book lay. They stepped on one another, jostled each other, began to snatch the pen from one another, dripped ink onto the book, and at last Bay Ganyo’s trembling, hairy, and sweaty hand adorned one of the pages with two sonorous words: Ganyo Balkanski
Tsvyatko told us that he did not wish to continue his story.
— Tell us something about the party. Didn’t you say they were giving a party in honor of the Bulgarians? — one of the group chimed in.

— I did not go to that party. Bay Ganyo did. A propos, on that day we went with Bay Ganyo to a barber shop. He had intended that evening to captivate the Czech ladies and was taking every possible precaution in advance to appear in all his splendor: he bought himself a tie, cleaned up his decorations (for how do you think your Bay Ganyo is!), and we went to the barber shop, since his hair and beard had grown quite long. He sat down in the chair. The barber carefully tied him up and began his work. We spent almost an entire hour there. It was not so easy to please Bay Ganyo.

— Here, here; tell him here — and Bay Ganyo points to his neck, — here to smooth it a bit, to scrape it a little with the razor. And tell him to keep his eyes open, so he doesn’t cut some pimple, or the devil take him.
Berberin sees through the mirror the angry expression on Bay Ganyo’s sweaty face and looks at me in bewilderment.

— What is he saying? — he asks me humbly, thinking he has made some mistake against Mr. Ganyo’s taste. — You tell him to stop the chatter for now — turns to me Mr. Ganyo, in such a tone as if he had hired me as a translator. — Tell him to leave me a little chin beard and make it a bit sharper, like Napoleon’s, do you understand? And as for the mustache, let him comb it so it stands out, like — heh, heh! — the Italian king’s, hee-hee-hee! Have you seen how he has it drawn? Let him make it like that! Tell him, will you!

I did not have the courage to translate literally old Bay Ganyo’s modest wish; it would have placed the barber in great difficulty: is it an easy task, with the help of a razor and a comb, to make someone resemble both Napoleon III and Humbert! And whom?

The haircut was over. Bay Ganyo took out his purse, twisted it around the cord, opened it, reached to the bottom, scooped up a handful of coins, turned his back to us, rummaged, rummaged through the coins, picked one out and handed it to the barber, but he handed it in such a way as if he wanted to say: “Come on then, there, let it go from me.” The coin was twenty kreuzers. But then, remembering that he might have made a mistake, and also so they wouldn’t think him a fool, he motioned with his fingers toward the barber, meaning, “give me the change.” The barber, in a second, opened the drawer, threw the coin in there, picked out two ten-kreuzer coins, slammed them angrily onto the marble table, and disappeared through an inner door. The coins rolled onto the floor. Bay Ganyo, at first, seemed to startle, to wonder, but I did not manage to catch that impression, and he bent down, picked up the money, and said:

— Angry Petko — his little bag is empty! Come on now, leave them be! They only know how to fleece people! I know them well! Slavs!... Nonsense!...
